title: Gradient - the direction of steepest ascent

questions.prompt: The gradient of a loss function points in the direction of steepest ASCENT. Why does gradient descent subtract it?
options: Because subtraction is cheaper than addition
Because the gradient is always negative
Because the gradient tells you which way the loss grows fastest, so moving against it is the way the loss shrinks
Because subtracting avoids overflow
questions.explain: The gradient is the uphill direction, so w -= lr * dL/dw walks downhill - that is the update in examples/03_train_linear.py. The tempting wrong answer is the second one: the gradient's sign depends on the error, and the file's own sign sanity check shows it pointing both ways depending on whether the prediction was too high or too low.

questions.prompt: In logistic regression, dL/dw_i = (p - y) * p * (1 - p) * x_i. Where does the chain rule come in?
options: The factor (p - y) is the chain rule applied twice
The factor x_i is the chain rule, since z = w . x + b
There is no chain rule here - the gradient is derived directly from the loss alone
The three local derivatives along the path loss -> p -> z -> w are multiplied together: (p - y)/(p(1-p)) times p(1-p) times x_i, and the sigmoid's p(1-p) cancels against the loss's 1/(p(1-p))
questions.explain: The chain rule multiplies the local derivatives along the path, and in this case the sigmoid's derivative p(1-p) cancels the loss's own 1/(p(1-p)), leaving the neat product. The tempting wrong answer is the second one: x_i is indeed dz/dw_i, but it is one of three factors in a product, not the chain rule by itself.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a partial derivative and the gradient?
options: A partial derivative is the derivative of a multi-variable function with respect to one variable, holding the others fixed; the gradient is the collection of all those partial derivatives, one per parameter
A partial derivative is for functions of one variable; the gradient is for functions of many variables
They are the same thing in different notation
The gradient is the numerical approximation and the partial derivative is the exact value
questions.explain: A partial derivative is one slope, one coordinate at a time; the gradient is the whole vector of them, shaped like the parameter vector. The tempting wrong answer is the last one: it is the opposite of the truth - the partial derivative is the exact analytic value, and the numeric finite-difference estimate is the approximation you use to CHECK it.

questions.prompt: Why does a confidently-wrong model learn so slowly?
options: Because the gradient's sign is wrong when the model is confident
Because the loss becomes infinite and the optimiser stops
Because the factor p * (1 - p) vanishes as p approaches 0 or 1, so the examples the model gets wrong contribute almost nothing to the update - the direction is right, the step size is nearly zero
Because the learning rate is automatically reduced for saturated models
questions.explain: The p(1-p) factor is at most 0.25 and goes to zero at the extremes: at p = 0.99 it is 0.0099. So the gradient magnitude collapses on exactly the examples that need correcting - the vanishing-gradient problem in its simplest form. The tempting wrong answer is the second one: the loss is large but finite (unless p hits exactly 0, and the file clamps it), so training continues - it just moves almost not at all on the wrong examples.

questions.prompt: Why can this repo's injection and friction batteries run without gold labels, while the routing battery cannot?
options: Because the gradient needs a label: dL/dp contains y, so without a gold answer there is no error to measure - and the friction and injection batteries measure the OUTPUT, not the error
Because the injection and friction cases are easier
Because the routing battery's labels are stored somewhere else
Because providers compute their own gradients
questions.explain: dL/dp = (p - y) / (p(1-p)) contains the label y. Without a label there is no loss and no gradient - which is exactly why harness.run_battery() only calls metrics.score_case() when a case has a gold key, and why run_format_friction() never needs one. The tempting wrong answer is the second one: it is not about difficulty, it is about what is being measured.
